extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter that recites a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or product of nature) is integrated into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two of the Alice/Mayo test. Includes criteria and considerations examiners should apply and illustrative case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics (product of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'markedly different' a characteristic must be changed as compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic or an incidental change; applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and the change came about or was produced by applicant’s efforts or influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product of nature exception. Examples: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and new hydrocarbon-degrading capacity deemed markedly different); Myriad (full-length cDNA with exon-only sequence deemed not a product of nature). Anti-examples: isolated genes (Myriad) and primers (Ambry) lacked sufficient marked difference because structural/function characteristics remained innate or incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that are incidental (e.g., isolation) or characteristics that are innate to the natural material do not rise to the level of a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated BRCA genes lost covalent end bonds but were otherwise structurally identical and thus not markedly different. Ambry: synthetically created single-stranded primers had the same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function, so they lacked markedly different characteristics. Roslin: animal clones were genetic replicas; alleged phenotypic differences were not claimed and therefore did not make the clones markedly different. See also In re Marden (ductility inherent characteristic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two - integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining a claim recites a judicial exception in Step 2A Prong One, evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application, the claim is not 'directed to' the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible (Pathway B). If not, the claim is directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B (inventive concept). The analysis evaluates whether additional elements impose a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of elements) indicative of integration is an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to another technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving computer/technology functioning meaningfully limits the claim beyond merely linking to a technological environment and can render the claim not 'directed to' the exception. Examiners should evaluate the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient detail for one of ordinary skill in the art to recognize the improvement, and then ensure the claim includes components/steps that provide that improvement. The specification need not explicitly assert the improvement, but a conclusory assertion without detail is insufficient. Examples: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system), Finjan (virus scanning security profile). Note: the Step 2A improvement analysis does not ignore whether activity is conventional (unlike Step 2B), i.e., a claimed improvement may integrate the exception even if it involves well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying/using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that applies or uses the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration requires that the claim limitation affirmatively recite an action that is a treatment or prophylaxis (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient'). Merely reciting intended use or field-of-use (e.g., 'prescribing', 'a pharmaceutical composition') or a non-affirmative recitation (e.g., 'is operable to be used') does not qualify. Example: Vanda (genotyping followed by genotype-dependent dosing for iloperidone held to integrate law of nature into a particular treatment and thus not directed to the exception). Factors to consider include the particularity vs generality of the treatment (a specific dosing step integrates the exception; a generic 'administering a suitable medication' does not) and whether the limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: implementing the exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Using or implementing a judicial exception with, or in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim can indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(b). The mere recitation of a generic machine is not automatically sufficient; the machine must be integral to how the claimed invention applies the exception (not just using a computer as a tool).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing supports integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to the 'particular machine' consideration and is discussed further in MPEP § 2106.05(c). The claimed transformation should be substantive and tied to the exception's application, not merely incidental or nominal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying/using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond merely linking to technology or field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying or using the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment or field of use may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all for additional meaningful limitations that prevent the claim from being merely a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for examples and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that do not integrate a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of additional elements have been identified by courts as not integrating a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: merely reciting the words 'apply it' or equivalent instructions to implement an abstract idea (or merely using a computer as a tool) (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)); adding insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)); and generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (MPEP § 2106.05(h)). Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not itself sufficient for eligibility (Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight to all additional elements (conventionality not dispositive at Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A Prong Two examiners should give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional; additional elements that represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity may nevertheless integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Step 2B where conventionality is a key inquiry, Prong Two requires evaluating whether additional elements (even if conventional) meaningfully limit the exception. Examiners must not ignore conventional elements when evaluating integration. However, mere physical implementation (tangibility) is not determinative of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of achieving a result is not standalone but can inform other considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific way of achieving a result is not by itself a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two, but specificity of limitations is relevant to evaluating particular machine use, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to explain specifics (e.g., how to select parameters, monitor processes, or implement steps) can suggest that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity (Parker v. Flook). Thus examiners should consider whether the claim explains sufficient specifics of how the result is achieved when assessing whether limitations meaningfully integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners evaluate integration into a practical application by (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the considerations provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim; the analysis is not a weighing test. Examiners should evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and consider how the limitations interact when evaluating integration. Each claim must be examined separately; dependent claims may be eligible even if independent claims are not, if they recite additional elements that amount to significantly more or that integrate the exception into a practical application. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1)-(2) and 2106.05(a)-(h) for further detail and examples (e.g., Solutran, Finjan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs generality of treatment/prophylaxis limitations (factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing a treatment/prophylaxis limitation, consider whether the treatment/prophylaxis is particular (specific) or general (generic); particular limitations are more likely to integrate the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mentally analyzing genotype and then 'administering a lower than normal dosage' is particular and integrates the mental process into a practical application; 'administering a suitable medication' is generic and does not. Examiners may also evaluate related considerations such as whether a limitation is merely an instruction to apply the exception or a generic field-of-use limitation.
